seo.best_title: Why Did Ancient Humans Start Wearing Clothes?
seo.description_hook: Why did ancient humans start wearing clothes, and when? The best clue comes from an unexpected place: lice. Plus the first needle, a 5,000 year old dress, and a snail worth more than gold.
paragraphs: In this animated history of clothing we look at why humans lost their body hair, how early humans survived the ice age, and how body lice DNA reveals when people first started wearing clothes.

Then we visit 120,000 year old hide-working tools in Morocco, Neanderthal capes, the 50,000 year old bone needle from Denisova Cave, the beaded burials of Sungir, 30,000 year old dyed flax fibers, and Otzi the Iceman's outfit.

We finish with the oldest trousers (made for horse riders), Tutankhamun's 145 loincloths, the Tarkhan Dress, the oldest leather shoe, Chinese silk, Roman togas and Tyrian purple dye, buttons and zippers, and the real reasons humans wear clothes.

Kittler, Kayser & Stoneking - Molecular evolution of Pediculus humanus and the origin of clothing, Current Biology (2003)
Rogers, Iltis & Wooding - Genetic variation at the MC1R locus and the time since loss of human body hair, Current Anthropology (2004)
Hallett et al. - A worked bone assemblage from 120,000-90,000 year old deposits at Contrebandiers Cave, Morocco, iScience (2021)
Kvavadze et al. - 30,000-year-old wild flax fibers, Science (2009)
Ian Gilligan - Climate, Clothing, and Agriculture in Prehistory (2019)
O'Sullivan et al. - A whole mitochondria analysis of the Tyrolean Iceman's leather, Scientific Reports (2016)
Stevenson et al. - The date of the earliest linen dress, Antiquity (2016)
Pinhasi et al. - First direct evidence of chalcolithic footwear from the Near Eastern highlands, PLOS ONE (2010)
Beck et al. - The invention of trousers and its likely affiliation with horseback riding and mobility, Quaternary International (2014)
Splitstoser et al. - Early pre-Hispanic use of indigo blue in Peru, Science Advances (2016)

shots.say: Right now, as you're watching this, you are almost certainly wearing clothes.
Maybe a hoodie. Maybe pajamas. Maybe something you really should have washed by now.
And you're not alone. Pretty much all eight billion of us got dressed today,
and most of us didn't think about it for even a second.
But here's a weird thing. We're the only animal that does this.

shots.title: WHO WEARS CLOTHES?
shots.say: Cats don't. Apes don't. And if your dog wears a sweater, that was your idea, not his.
Sorry, buddy.
So at some point, a very long time ago, a human looked at an animal skin and thought,
you know what? I'm going to wear that.
And that moment is older than writing, older than farming, older than any city on Earth.
And the best clue we have for when it happened comes from... lice.
Yes. The tiny bugs. We'll get there, I promise.

shots.title: TODAY
shots.say: Along the way, we'll find out why we lost our fur, how bugs became historians, and why a snail was worth more than gold.
So get comfortable. Clothes optional. Let's go.

shots.say: Okay, first question. Why do we even need clothes in the first place?
Look at a chimpanzee. Covered in fur, head to toe. Now look at yourself in the mirror.
Mostly not covered in fur. Hopefully.
Somewhere along the way, our ancestors lost almost all of their body hair.
And scientists think it happened more than a million years ago.
Which raises the obvious question. How on earth do you date a missing thing?

shots.title: THE SKIN CLUE
shots.say: The answer is skin color. Under thick fur, skin can stay pale. But take the fur away under the African sun,
and you need dark skin to protect you. Genes for that dark skin go back over a million years.
So by then, the fur was mostly gone. But why lose it at all?

shots.title: WHY NO FUR?
shots.say: There are a few ideas. Sweating keeps you cool. Staying cool lets you chase animals for hours. And less fur means fewer places for bugs to live.
Early humans could jog after an animal in the midday heat until it simply collapsed.
shots.ai: a sweating early human jogging after a deer across a hot savanna

shots.say: We basically became the sweatiest marathon runners in the animal kingdom.
Scientists still argue about which reason mattered most. Honestly, probably all of them a bit.
But losing your fur works great in Africa. The rest of the world, though? Not always so warm.

shots.label: OUT OF AFRICA
shots.say: Because over time, our ancestors spread out of Africa and across the planet.
Into Europe and Asia, where the winters could be absolutely brutal.
shots.ai: a shivering stick figure standing in a snowy ice age landscape

shots.say: And a lot of that happened during an ice age.
So imagine walking into an ice age with no fur, no coat, no nothing.
That's not a bold fashion choice. That's a survival problem.
So clothes probably started as survival gear. Fashion came later.
The tricky part is that clothes rot. Leather and fur don't last a hundred thousand years in the ground.
So how do we figure out when people started wearing them? That's where the bugs come in.

shots.say: Now here's the weird part.
Humans have two main kinds of lice. Head lice, which live in your hair,
and body lice, which actually live in your clothes. Lovely, I know.
And body lice can't really survive without clothing. No clothes, no home.

shots.title: THE LOGIC
shots.say: So at some point, when people started wearing clothes, some head lice moved in, and slowly became a new kind of louse.
Which means if you can figure out when body lice split from head lice,
you can figure out roughly when clothes appeared.
That's exactly what scientists did, by comparing the DNA of lice.
shots.label: LICE DNA
shots.ai: a scientist stick figure studying a louse through a magnifying glass in a lab

shots.say: A big study in 2011 found the split happened at least eighty-three thousand years ago,
and maybe as early as a hundred and seventy thousand years ago.
And it happened in Africa, before people left. So humans were already dressed when they set out.
So, in a way, the first historians of fashion were bugs.
The exact numbers are still debated, of course. But it's the best clue we've got.

shots.say: And then there are the tools.

shots.label: CONTREBANDIERS CAVE
shots.say: In a cave on the coast of Morocco, archaeologists found a collection of carefully shaped bone tools.
Some of them are around a hundred and twenty thousand years old.
And they were made for one very specific job: scraping and smoothing animal hides.
shots.ai: an early human scraping an animal hide with a bone tool in a cave

shots.title: MAKING LEATHER
shots.say: Basically, you take an animal, scrape the hide clean, work it until it's soft, and boom. Leather.
They also found bones of foxes and wildcats with cut marks from skinning,
not for the meat, but for the fur.
So, the first fashion workshop. Very fluffy. And, I imagine, very smelly.

shots.say: What about the Neanderthals? They lived in ice age Europe for hundreds of thousands of years.
They definitely covered up. But probably with fairly simple things, like big wraps and capes.
shots.ai: a Neanderthal wearing a simple fur cape standing in the snow by a fire

shots.say: Think of a big, heavy blanket thrown over your shoulders.
Warm-ish, sure. But loose. And the wind gets in absolutely everywhere.
It's like trying to survive a snowstorm in a bath towel.
Some researchers think this mattered in the coldest times. Others say Neanderthals were tough enough. It's still argued about.
But our own ancestors had a tiny invention that changed everything.

Let me guess. A leopard skin over one shoulder, and a big wooden club.

In a real ice age, that outfit would get you killed. Fast.
Real ice age people needed covered arms, covered legs, boots, and hoods.
shots.ai: a stick figure in a warm hooded fur parka in a snowy landscape

shots.say: Think less cartoon caveman, more serious outdoor gear expert.
Somebody please tell the cartoon studios.

shots.say: So what was the invention? The sewing needle.
It sounds boring, I know. But a needle with an eye lets you do something new.

shots.title: FITTED CLOTHES
shots.say: You can cut pieces of hide and sew them tightly together, into clothes that actually fit your body.

shots.label: DENISOVA CAVE
shots.say: One of the oldest needles we know of was found in Denisova Cave, in Siberia.
It's made from bird bone, and it's somewhere around fifty thousand years old.
And suddenly, you've got sleeves. Leggings. Hoods. No more drafty capes.
With properly sewn clothes, people could survive in places like the Arctic.
shots.ai: two stick figures in sewn fur parkas waving next to a mammoth in a snowy tundra

shots.say: So honestly, the humble needle might be one of the most important inventions ever made.
Right up there with fire, the wheel, and Wi-Fi.

shots.say: But clothes were never just about staying warm.

shots.label: SUNGIR
shots.say: Take a site called Sungir, in Russia. It's about thirty-four thousand years old.
Archaeologists found a man and two children buried in clothes covered in ivory beads.
shots.label: SUNGIR BURIAL

shots.say: Not a few beads. Thousands of them. Each one carved by hand.
Researchers estimate each bead took around an hour to make.
So we're talking thousands of hours of work, just on decoration.
Which tells us clothes were already about something else too. Status. Identity. Who you were.
The Stone Age had designer outfits. Prices available on request.

shots.say: Animals gave people leather and fur. But plants gave them something else entirely.

shots.label: DZUDZUANA CAVE
shots.say: In a cave in the country of Georgia, scientists found tiny fibers of flax.
About thirty thousand years old.

shots.title: FLAX TO FABRIC
shots.say: Flax can be twisted into string, and string can be woven into cloth.
And here's the fun part. Some of the fibers were dyed. Black, gray, even pink and turquoise.
Thirty thousand years ago, somebody really wanted something in pink.
To be fair, those fibers might have been for cords or baskets too. We can't be sure.
But little statues from around this time do show what look like woven caps and hats.

shots.say: And once people had cloth, of course, they wanted color.

shots.title: ANCIENT DYES
shots.say: Red earth called ochre. All kinds of plants. And, as we'll see later, snails.

shots.say: In Peru, archaeologists found scraps of cotton cloth dyed blue with indigo,
and they're about six thousand years old. The oldest indigo dye we know of.
Indigo is the same dye family that's used to color denim today.
So your blue jeans have a six-thousand-year-old color history.

shots.say: Now, let me throw a bold idea at you.
Why did humans start farming? Most people would say: food, obviously.
But an archaeologist named Ian Gilligan has suggested there might be another reason.
shots.label: IAN GILLIGAN

shots.title: THE CLOTHES THEORY
shots.say: People needed huge amounts of material for clothes. Animals for hides and wool. Plants for fiber.
So maybe farming was partly about clothes, and not only about food.
Which would mean agriculture was, at least partly, a fashion decision.
Most experts aren't convinced, to be honest. It's a minority view. But it's a fun one to think about.

shots.label: OTZI
shots.say: Fast forward to 1991. Two hikers in the Alps spot something sticking out of the ice.
It's a man. And he's been there for about five thousand three hundred years. They named him Otzi.
And the amazing thing is, he still had his clothes on.
shots.ai: Otzi the iceman in his leather and fur clothing standing in the Alps

shots.title: OTZI'S OUTFIT
shots.say: A goat hide coat. A bearskin hat. A cape made of grass. And leather leggings.
His clothes were made from at least five different kinds of animal.
And his shoes were stuffed with grass, to keep his feet warm. Basically ancient insulation.
Honestly? He was better dressed for winter than I am.

shots.say: Meanwhile, down in Egypt, it was a completely different story. Too hot for furs.
People mostly wore linen. And the oldest woven dress in the world comes from there: the Tarkhan Dress.
shots.label: TARKHAN DRESS

shots.say: It's over five thousand years old. And it has pleats.
Pleats. Somebody carefully pleated this five thousand years ago.
Egyptian kids, on the other hand, often wore nothing at all. It was just too hot.
And a lot of wealthy Egyptians shaved their heads and wore wigs instead.
Partly to stay cool and clean. And partly because of... you guessed it. Lice.

shots.say: Here's a question nobody ever asks. Who invented pants?
Because for most of history, people wore robes, wraps, tunics, and skirts. Not trousers.

shots.label: YANGHAI
shots.say: The oldest trousers we know of were found in a cemetery in western China,
and they're roughly three thousand years old.
They belonged to a man who was buried with his horse gear. He was a rider.
shots.ai: an ancient horse rider in early woolen trousers next to his horse on the steppe

shots.say: And that's the secret. Pants were invented for riding horses.
If you've ever tried to ride a horse in a long robe, you'll understand why. Very quickly.
The Greeks and Romans actually thought pants looked ridiculous. Barbarian clothing.
So next time you put on your jeans, take a moment to thank a horse.

shots.say: And what about your feet?

shots.label: ARENI-1
shots.say: In a cave in Armenia, archaeologists found the oldest leather shoe ever discovered.
It's around five thousand five hundred years old.
Made from a single piece of cowhide, laced up the front, and stuffed with grass.
shots.label: ARENI SHOE

shots.say: And it's roughly a modern women's size 7. Someone today could actually wear it.

shots.label: FORT ROCK
shots.say: And in Oregon, woven sandals have been found that are even older. Around nine thousand years.
So comfortable footwear? Also older than writing.

shots.label: CHINA
shots.say: Back in China, people discovered something incredible. Silk.

shots.title: SILK
shots.say: Silkworms eat mulberry leaves, then spin cocoons made of one long, super fine thread.
Chemical traces suggest people were using silk over eight thousand years ago.
And China kept the secret of making it for centuries. Silk was worth a fortune.
It traveled west along the trade routes we now call the Silk Road.
Rich Romans loved it so much that some writers complained it was basically see-through.

shots.say: Speaking of Rome. Let's talk about the famous toga.

shots.label: TOGA

Some of them were around six meters of cloth.

So many Romans just didn't want to wear it. Emperors actually had to order people to.
And the most expensive color in Rome? Purple.

shots.title: TYRIAN PURPLE

You needed thousands of snails to dye even a small piece of cloth.
So purple became the color of emperors. Literally, royal purple.
Fun fact: the dye workshops smelled horrible. Thousands of rotting snails. Glamorous.

shots.say: Now, how did people keep all these clothes on? For most of history: belts, pins, and knots.
Buttons came surprisingly late.

shots.label: INDUS VALLEY
shots.say: Some of the oldest button-like objects come from the Indus Valley, about five thousand years ago,
but they were just decorations. Not for closing anything.
Buttons with buttonholes only really took off in Europe around eight hundred years ago.
And the modern zipper? Barely a hundred years old.
So for almost all of history, nobody ever got their zipper stuck. Lucky them.

scenes.chapter: So Why Do We Wear Clothes?

shots.say: So let's go back to the big question. Why did humans start wearing clothes?

shots.title: THE REASONS
shots.say: Warmth. Protection. Status. And later on, modesty.
Warmth almost certainly came first. When it's freezing, survival comes first.
But decoration and status showed up very early too. Remember those beads at Sungir.
And modesty? That changes a lot depending on where and when you lived.
In some hot places, people wore very little for thousands of years, and that was completely normal.
